fuentes/decreto-de-priene-para-sotas/tit.texto: Decree of Priene in honour of Sotas

fuentes/decreto-de-priene-para-sotas/res.texto: Decree of the Greek city of Priene, in Ionia, which honours Sotas for having gathered citizens on horseback and rescued those who were in the countryside when the Galatians, newly arrived in Asia, were plundering the territory. It describes the Galatians for their impiety towards the temples and their cruelty to prisoners.

fuentes/decreto-de-priene-para-sotas/por.texto: It is a contemporary witness to the first years of the Galatians in Asia Minor, and it confirms the raids described by Livy (XXXVIII.16). Its language of “impiety” and “savagery” is the same that Greek cities used to describe any barbarian enemy, and for that reason it tells us as much about fear as about events.

fuentes/dedicatorias-de-atalo-i/titulo.texto: Dedications of Attalus I for his victories over the Galatians

fuentes/dedicatorias-de-atalo-i/resumen.texto: Inscriptions on the bases of the monuments that Attalus I set up in the sanctuary of Athena Nikephoros at Pergamon. One reads: “King Attalus, victorious in battle over the Tolistoboian Galatians by the springs of the river Caicus, to Athena, in thanks”. The series on one long base lists his victories over the Galatians, over Antiochus Hierax and over the generals of Seleucus III. They were published by Max Fränkel in 1890; some bear the signature of Epigonus.

fuentes/dedicatorias-de-atalo-i/por_que_.texto: They are the testimony of the victor himself: they show that Attalus built his kingship on victory over the Galatians, and they are the basis for dating the monuments from which the Dying Gaul and the Ludovisi Gaul would come. Several are broken and restored, and their exact date, between about 240 and 223 BC, is debated.

fuentes/galatas-en-abidos/titulo.texto: Galatian graffito in the temple of Seti I at Abydos

fuentes/galatas-en-abidos/resumen.texto: Greek graffito left by mercenaries in the temple of Seti I at Abydos, in Upper Egypt: “Of the Galatians, Thoas, Callistratus, Acanon, Apollonius: we came and hunted a fox here”. It was edited by Dittenberger (OGIS 757) among the graffiti of the Memnonion at Abydos. It is dated to around 186-185 BC, when Ptolemy V was using Galatian troops against the revolt in Upper Egypt.

fuentes/galatas-en-abidos/por_que_import.texto: It is one of the few texts written by the Celtic mercenaries of the Hellenistic world themselves, and the fact that three of the four names are Greek shows how quickly they became Hellenized. Philip Freeman uses it as proof that some Galatians were writing in Greek a few decades after their arrival. Stephen Colvin (Bryn Mawr Classical Review, 2002) objected that the speech of a few mercenaries in a Hellenistic army says little about what was happening in the Galatia of Anatolia.

fuentes/galatas-en-abidos/leer.0.titulo.texto: Greek text in the Packard Humanities Institute database of Greek inscriptions

fuentes/pro-rege-deiotaro/resumen.texto: Speech that Cicero delivered in November 45 BC before Julius Caesar, in Caesar's house, in defence of the Galatian king Deiotarus, accused by his grandson Castor of having plotted to kill Caesar when he hosted him in Galatia in 47 BC. Cicero ridicules the accusation and the accuser, recalls Deiotarus' services to Rome against Mithridates and his friendship with Pompey, and paints the king as a loyal, sober and Hellenized ally.

fuentes/pro-rege-deiotaro/por_que_import.texto: It is one of the few contemporary sources on a Galatian king, and it shows how the Galatian aristocracy moved within Roman politics. It is the plea of a lawyer and friend of the accused, written to acquit him, not a neutral description. Caesar never handed down a verdict, because he was killed in March 44 BC.

fuentes/pro-rege-deiotaro/leer.0.titulo.texto: Latin text at The Latin Library

fuentes/trofeo-de-los-alpes/titulo.texto: Inscription of the Trophy of the Alps

fuentes/trofeo-de-los-alpes/resumen.texto: Inscription of the monument that the Senate dedicated to Augustus in 7-6 BC at La Turbie, on the coast of the Maritime Alps, because under his command and auspices “all the Alpine peoples from the Upper Sea to the Lower Sea” were subdued by Rome. It continues with a list of more than forty defeated peoples, among them the four tribes of the Vindelici, the Salassi and the Ceutrones. Pliny the Elder (Natural History III.136-137) copied the full text, and that copy was used to reconstruct the fragments that remain on the site.

fuentes/trofeo-de-los-alpes/por_que_impo.texto: It is the official Roman list of the conquest of the Alps and a main source for the names of the Alpine peoples, Celtic, Raetian and Ligurian. It is a monument of propaganda: it combines in a single victory of Augustus campaigns from different years and generals, between 25 and 14 BC.

fuentes/trofeo-de-los-alpes/leer.0.titul.texto: Pliny, Natural History III, with the copy of the inscription in paragraphs 136-137 (Latin text at The Latin Library)

fuentes/geografia-de-estrabon-libro-xii/.texto: Describes the centre of Asia Minor: Cappadocia, Pontus, Bithynia, Galatia, Lycaonia, Pisidia and Phrygia. In XII.5.1-3 it recounts the organization of the Galatians: three peoples (Trocmi, Tolistoboii and Tectosages) with the same language, each divided into four tetrarchies with its tetrarch, its judge and its military chief, and a council of three hundred that met at the place called Drunemeton and judged homicides. It also explains how in his time power passed from twelve tetrarchs to three and then to one alone, Deiotarus. It also describes Pessinus and the sanctuary of the Great Mother, Ancyra and Tavium.

It is almost the only source on Galatian institutions and the basis for everything said about the Drunemeton, whose name is usually interpreted as “sanctuary of the oaks” or “great sanctuary” (Celtic nemeton, “sacred place”). Strabo was from Amaseia, a neighbour of Galatia, and knew the region, but he describes an order that no longer existed when he wrote, and the symmetry of twelve tetrarchies may be idealized.
English translation at Perseus (book XII, chapter on Galatia)

fuentes/historia-de-heraclea-memnon/resu.texto: History of the Greek city of Heraclea Pontica, on the southern coast of the Black Sea, preserved only in the summary of books IX to XVI made by the patriarch Photius in his Bibliotheca (codex 224). It recounts the death of Ptolemy Ceraunus at the hands of the Gauls, who knocked him down with his wounded elephant (8.8); the agreement of Nicomedes I with the Gallic chiefs to bring them into Asia, with its clauses; and the wars of Heraclea against the Galatians.

fuentes/historia-de-heraclea-memnon/por_.texto: It is the closest and most detailed source on the treaty that brought the Galatians to Asia Minor, because Memnon used local historians such as Nymphis of Heraclea, who lived in the 3rd century BC. But it reaches us at third hand, summarized by a Byzantine reader, and it contains confusions: it assigns Ancyra to the Trocmi and Pessinus to the Tectosages (11.7), the reverse of Strabo.

fuentes/historia-de-heraclea-memnon/leer.texto: English translation by Andrew Smith (2004), chapters 1 to 21, on the translator's site (requires a browser check)

fuentes/alejandro-o-el-falso-profeta/res.texto: Satirical pamphlet against Alexander of Abonuteichos, a diviner from Paphlagonia who founded the cult of the serpent Glycon, and whom Lucian knew and hated. In one passage (51) he says that Alexander answered oracles for foreigners in their own language, Syrian or Celtic, because he found people of his own nation in the city who served as his interpreters.

fuentes/alejandro-o-el-falso-profeta/por.texto: It is one of the indications that in the 2nd century AD Celtic was still spoken in Asia Minor, although Lucian does not say that those Celts were Galatians and gives no word of their language. It is satire, written against a personal enemy.

fuentes/vida-de-eutimio/resumen.texto: Biography of Euthymius (377-473), an Armenian monk who founded lauras in the Judean desert, written by Cyril from the memories of the oldest monks. Among the miracles (chapter 55) he tells of a possessed Galatian monk who did not speak and who, if pressed, “spoke in Galatian”.

fuentes/vida-de-eutimio/por_que_importa.texto: It is the latest testimony to Galatian as a spoken language, and the one that allows us to say it may have survived into the 6th century. But it is an isolated miracle story, about a single monk and without a single word of the language, and so how long Galatian continued to be spoken remains under discussion.

fuentes/sentencia-del-robo-del-oro-de-ma.texto: Judgment of the Ingolstadt Regional Court on the theft of the Manching gold

Press release from the court's first criminal chamber on the judgment of 29 July 2025, handed down after thirty-three hearings. The four defendants were convicted of a series of break-ins committed by force over a long period in different regions, among other offences for aggravated gang theft, and received sentences of between four years and nine months and eleven years in prison. One was acquitted of the Manching offence because the chamber was not convinced of his guilt. The conviction rested on circumstantial evidence: eighteen pieces of melted gold that experts attributed to the treasure, tools, DNA and phone traces, surveillance videos and a repeated modus operandi.

It closes the judicial case over the theft of the Celtic gold coins from the Manching museum. The press release clarifies that the judgment was not final; the Federal Court of Justice essentially rejected the appeals in August 2026, and the sentences became final. Most of the coins have still not been recovered.
Press release of the Ingolstadt Regional Court

fuentes/les-galates-en-grece-nachtergael.texto: The Galatians in Greece and the Soteria of Delphi

A study of the Gallic invasion of Greece and of the Soteria festivals, based on the inscriptions of Delphi and the historians, with a corpus of the epigraphic documents, among them the decree of Cos. It distinguishes the first Soteria, amphictyonic, celebrated from shortly after 278 BC, from the Aetolian Soteria, reorganized as a Panhellenic festival around 246 BC, and reconstructs the chronology of the invasion.

It is the reference work on the subject and shows how much of the story of the rescue of Delphi was built in the decrees of the Aetolians, who controlled the sanctuary. The exact date of the Aetolian reorganization and the weight of Aetolian propaganda in the epigraphic record are still debated, for example in Craige Champion's article of 1995.

fuentes/the-galatian-language-freeman/ti.texto: The Galatian Language: A Comprehensive Survey of the Language of the Ancient Celts in Greco-Roman Asia Minor

fuentes/the-galatian-language-freeman/re.texto: It gathers the ancient testimonies about the Galatians and their language and the known Galatian names (of persons, tribes, gods and places), with commentary. It concludes that only a few glosses and proper names of Galatian survive, that it was very close to Gaulish, and that it coexisted with Greek for centuries.

fuentes/the-galatian-language-freeman/po.texto: It is the standard collection on Galatian. Stephen Colvin, in his review in the Bryn Mawr Classical Review (2002), criticized it for being more a corpus of names than a linguistic study, for leaving the Greek and Latin texts untranslated and containing some errors, for assuming that the whole population was bilingual for centuries without addressing the complexity of bilingualism, and for etymologies that are not well founded.

fuentes/oppida-collis-1984/titulo.texto: Oppida: Earliest Towns North of the Alps

fuentes/oppida-collis-1984/resumen.texto: A synthesis of the archaeology of the oppida of temperate Europe, such as Manching, Stradonice, Závist and Bibracte: large walled enclosures of the 2nd and 1st centuries BC, with specialized craftwork, coinage and trade with the Mediterranean. Collis argues that they were the first towns north of the Alps, arising from the growth of production and trade.

fuentes/oppida-collis-1984/por_que_impor.texto: It fixed the use of the word “town” for the oppida, which has been debated ever since. Greg Woolf (1993) objected that many had large empty spaces and short lives, and that copying the model of the Mediterranean city obscures their function, which may have been more political and ceremonial than urban.

fuentes/rethinking-the-oppida-woolf-1993.texto: An article in the Oxford Journal of Archaeology that questions whether the oppida were cities in the Mediterranean sense: many enclosed large unbuilt spaces and lasted only a short time, and their emergence is better explained by changes in elite power and by contact with Rome than by a process of urbanization.

It opened the debate on the nature of the oppida. Later authors, such as Manuel Fernández-Götz, replied that, although discontinuous and of low density, many oppida performed urban functions, and that the definition of a city should not be taken from the Mediterranean alone.

fuentes/urbanizacion-edad-del-hierro-fer.texto: Urbanization in Iron Age Europe: Trajectories, Patterns, and Social Dynamics

A review published in the Journal of Archaeological Research that describes two waves of urbanization in temperate Europe, separated by a return to rural life: the Hallstatt “princely” centres of the 6th and 5th centuries BC, such as Heuneburg, and the oppida of the 2nd and 1st centuries BC, such as Manching. It argues that the process was discontinuous, with low-density forms, in which sanctuaries and assemblies played a central role.

It is the most cited synthesis of the current approach, which accepts calling the oppida urban without copying them from the Mediterranean. Woolf's sceptical position still carries weight, because the population figures for the oppida, such as the five to ten thousand inhabitants estimated for Manching, are estimates with wide margins.
Open-access article in the Journal of Archaeological Research

fuentes/ludovisi-barbarians-marvin-2002/.texto: The Ludovisi Barbarians: The Grand Manner

A chapter in The Ancient Art of Emulation, edited by Elaine Gazda, on the Ludovisi Gaul and the Dying Gaul, found in Rome in the gardens of Sallust. Marvin shows everything that separates these sculptures from their supposed Pergamene models, and considers them Roman creations of the 2nd century AD, in the “grand style” of Pergamon, related in style to the reliefs of the columns of Trajan and Marcus Aurelius.

It questions the basis on which art history reconstructs the monuments of Attalus I. The most widespread view still sees these statues as copies or adaptations of Pergamene originals, on the basis of what Pliny says (XXXIV.84) and of the bases signed by Epigonus.

fuentes/tesoro-de-duchcov-kruta/titulo.texto: The Duchcov hoard in the Czechoslovak collections

fuentes/tesoro-de-duchcov-kruta/resumen.texto: A catalogue and study of the pieces from the Duchcov deposit that are held in museums in Czechoslovakia: brooches, bracelets and rings of early La Tène bronze, found in 1882 inside a bronze cauldron in a spring. Kruta arranges them by type and dates them to the 4th century BC.

fuentes/tesoro-de-duchcov-kruta/por_que_.texto: The find gave its name to the “Duchcov-type brooch”, which serves to trace the Celtic expansion of the 4th century BC across central Europe, and this catalogue is the basis for studying it. The reading of the deposit as an offering in water is the most accepted, but the pieces were scattered after the find, and their original number and arrangement are not known.

fuentes/tumba-de-ciumesti-rusu-1969/titu.texto: The Celtic princely tomb of Ciumești, in Romania

fuentes/tumba-de-ciumesti-rusu-1969/resu.texto: Publication, in the Bericht der Römisch-Germanischen Kommission, of the tomb found in 1961 at Ciumești, in northwestern Romania, with an iron helmet crowned by a bronze bird of prey with movable wings, a mail coat, greaves and spears. Rusu dated it to the 3rd century BC and attributed it to a Celtic warrior chief.

fuentes/tumba-de-ciumesti-rusu-1969/por_.texto: It is the standard publication of the Ciumești helmet, one of the most reproduced pieces of Celtic armament, and of one of the oldest known mail coats. The date of the tomb is still debated.

fuentes/biblioteca-historica-diodoro-lib.texto: Fragments of the book of the Library of History that dealt with the years of the Gallic invasion and the wars of Pyrrhus, preserved in Byzantine excerpts. They recount the death of Ptolemy Ceraunus at the hands of the Gauls (XXII.3), the entry of Brennus into Delphi, where he is said to have laughed at the Greeks for giving their gods human form in wood and stone, and his suicide after drinking a great deal of undiluted wine (XXII.9), and the plundering of the tombs of Aegae by the Galatians of Pyrrhus (XXII.12).

Together with Pausanias and Justin, it is one of the three ancient versions of the invasion. Diodorus wrote in the 1st century BC, compiling earlier historians, probably Hieronymus of Cardia for this period, and his text survives in fragments.

fuentes/guerra-de-alejandria/resumen.texto: A continuation of Caesar's commentaries on the civil war, which narrates the Alexandrian War and the campaigns of 47 BC in Asia Minor and Illyria. It tells that Deiotarus had a legion armed and trained in the Roman manner (34), that Pharnaces of Pontus defeated it at Nicopolis, and how Caesar defeated Pharnaces at Zela (68-77) with troops of Deiotarus among his own.

fuentes/guerra-de-alejandria/por_que_imp.texto: It is the testimony of how a Galatian king organized his army in the Roman manner, the origin of the Twenty-second legion Deiotariana. Its author is not certain; tradition attributes it to Aulus Hirtius and, like the other Caesarian commentaries, it favours Caesar.

fuentes/sacerdotes-de-ancira/titulo.texto: List of the priests of the imperial cult at Ancyra

fuentes/sacerdotes-de-ancira/autor.texto: Community of the Galatians of Ancyra

fuentes/sacerdotes-de-ancira/soporte.texto: Inscription on the wall of the temple of Augustus and Roma

fuentes/sacerdotes-de-ancira/resumen.texto: Inscription carved on the temple of Augustus and Roma at Ancyra, which lists, year by year, the priests of the imperial cult of the Galatian community and what each one donated: public banquets, distributions of oil, gladiatorial contests and wild-beast hunts. Among the first are sons of kings and tetrarchs, such as Pylaimenes, son of King Amyntas.

fuentes/sacerdotes-de-ancira/por_que_imp.texto: It shows the aristocracy of the three tribes turned, within a single generation, into priests of the emperor who pay for Roman spectacles, and it is the best source for the names of the Galatian nobility. The dates of each priesthood and the reconstruction of the damaged parts are debated.

fuentes/anatolia-mitchell/titulo.texto: Anatolia: Land, Men, and Gods in Asia Minor

fuentes/anatolia-mitchell/resumen.texto: A two-volume history of central Anatolia from the arrival of the Galatians to Late Antique Christianity, based mainly on inscriptions and on the author's fieldwork. The first volume deals with the settlement of the Galatians, their tribes and tetrarchies, the Roman province and rural life; the second with the Christianization of the region.

fuentes/anatolia-mitchell/por_que_import.texto: It is the reference work on ancient Galatia. It presents the Galatians as a people who kept their tribal organization and their language for centuries while their aristocracy became Hellenized and Romanized. That continuity rests on few testimonies, and later works, such as those of Altay Coşkun, discuss how much of Galatian identity was inherited from Europe and how much was formed in Anatolia itself.

personas/cambaules/resumen.texto: A Gallic chief who, according to Pausanias (X.19.5), led the first expedition of the Celts into Thrace, before the great invasion, and turned back because he did not feel strong enough to go on to Greece. Pausanias gives no date; it is usually placed around 300 BC. He is a figure about whom nothing else is known.

personas/bolgio/resumen.texto: A Gallic chief who in 280-279 BC invaded Macedonia and defeated and killed King Ptolemy Ceraunus, whose head, according to Justin (XXIV.5), he paraded on a spear. Justin calls him Belgius and Pausanias (X.19.7) Bolgius; the fragments of Diodorus (XXII.3) recount the king's defeat. After plundering the country he returned to the north without trying to stay.

personas/cerecio/resumen.texto: A Gallic chief who in 279 BC led the column that attacked the Thracians and the Triballi, while Bolgius went against Macedonia and Brennus and Acichorius against Paeonia, according to Pausanias (X.19.7). It is the only information we have about him.

personas/breno-de-delfos/nombre.texto: Brennus (leader of the invasion of Greece)

personas/breno-de-delfos/resumen.texto: A Gallic chief who in 279 BC led the main column of the invasion of Macedonia and Greece, forced the pass of Thermopylae by going round the Greeks through the mountains, and attacked Delphi. We know him only from much later Greek and Roman authors: Pausanias (X.19-23), Justin (XXIV.6-8) and fragments of Diodorus (XXII.9), who present him as a sacrilegious man who mocked the stone gods of the Greeks. Wounded, he killed himself: by drinking undiluted wine according to Pausanias (X.23.12), with a dagger according to Justin (XXIV.8), and after drinking a great deal of undiluted wine according to Diodorus (XXII.9). He should not be confused with the Brennus of the sack of Rome of around 390 BC; the old hypothesis that “Brennus” was a title and not a name has no firm support.

personas/acicorio/resumen.texto: A Gallic chief who shared with Brennus the command of the column that invaded Greece in 279 BC. According to Pausanias (X.19.7, X.22-23), he stayed behind with the bulk of the army and joined Brennus in the attack on Delphi, where he was given the rearguard. We know him almost only from Pausanias.

personas/batanato/resumen.texto: A Gallic chief who, according to Athenaeus (VI.25, citing Posidonius), led part of those who had attacked Delphi back to the Danube. His descendants were called Bathanatoi, and their route was “the road of Bathanatos”. Athenaeus adds that the Scordisci, his successors, did not let gold enter their land because of the sacrilege at Delphi, although they did plunder silver. It is a tradition that explains a name, but it links the Scordisci with the invasion of 279 BC.

personas/leonorio/resumen.texto: A Gallic chief who, together with Lutarius, separated from the army of Brennus, passed into Thrace and crossed into Asia in 278-277 BC, hired by Nicomedes I of Bithynia. According to Livy (XXXVIII.16), he crossed the Bosporus with Nicomedes' help, while Lutarius crossed by the Hellespont. Memnon of Heraclea preserves the treaty they signed with the Bithynian king.

personas/lutario/resumen.texto: A Gallic chief who, together with Leonnorius, left Brennus and crossed into Asia in 278-277 BC. According to Livy (XXXVIII.16), he took by surprise some ships carrying Macedonian envoys and with them crossed the Hellespont. Memnon of Heraclea (11.3) calls him Luturius and counts him, together with Leonnorius, as the most important of the seventeen Gallic chiefs.

personas/comontorio/resumen.texto: A Gallic chief who, after the invasion of 279 BC, did not follow on to Greece or to Asia and founded a kingdom in eastern Thrace with its capital at Tylis, according to Polybius (IV.46). From there he forced Byzantium to pay him tribute, which came to eighty talents a year.

personas/cavaro/resumen.texto: The last king of the Gauls of Tylis. Polybius (IV.46, 52; VIII.22) says that he had a royal and generous character, that he protected the Black Sea merchants and mediated in 220 BC in the war between Byzantium and Rhodes, but that he let himself be corrupted by a flatterer, Sostratus of Chalcedon. During his reign the Thracians revolted and destroyed the kingdom, around 212 BC.

personas/ptolomeo-cerauno/resumen.texto: Son of Ptolemy I of Egypt, set aside from the succession, who murdered Seleucus I in 281 BC and made himself king of Macedonia. In 279 BC he faced the Gauls of Bolgius after rejecting the aid of twenty thousand Dardanians and answering the Gallic envoys with contempt, according to Justin (XXIV.4-5). According to Justin, he fell wounded and captured and was beheaded; according to Memnon of Heraclea (8.8), the elephant he was riding was wounded and threw him down, and the Gauls captured him alive and tore him apart.

personas/sostenes-de-macedonia/resumen.texto: A Macedonian general who, after the death of Ptolemy Ceraunus, gathered an army and repelled the Gauls of Bolgius in 279 BC. According to Justin (XXIV.5), he did not accept the title of king and had himself sworn in only as general. Brennus defeated him shortly afterwards, and he died around 277 BC, amid the anarchy in Macedonia.

personas/antigono-ii-gonatas/resumen.texto: King of Macedonia from 277 to 239 BC, son of Demetrius Poliorcetes. His victory over a Gallic band near Lysimachia in 277 BC, which Justin recounts (XXV.1-2), gave him the prestige to be recognized as king of Macedonia, which had been without a ruler since the death of Ptolemy Ceraunus. He later used Gallic mercenaries in his wars and established the Antigonid dynasty in Macedonia, which ruled until 168 BC.

personas/nicomedes-i-de-bitinia/resumen.texto: King of Bithynia who, at war with Antiochus I and with his own brother, hired the Gauls of Leonnorius and Lutarius and brought them into Asia in 278-277 BC. Memnon of Heraclea (11) summarizes the treaty: the Gauls would always support Nicomedes and his sons, would not ally with anyone without his permission, and would also fight for Byzantium, Heraclea, Chalcedon, Tius and Cius. He founded Nicomedia around 264 BC.

personas/antioco-i-soter/resumen.texto: Seleucid king from 281 to 261 BC. According to Lucian (Zeuxis 8-11), he defeated the Galatians in the “battle of the elephants”, in which sixteen elephants frightened the Galatians' horses, which had never seen them, and Appian (Syriaca 65) says that the surname Soter, “saviour”, came to him from that victory. The date of the battle, between 275 and 268 BC, is debated.

personas/antioco-hierax/resumen.texto: Younger brother of the Seleucid king Seleucus II, who contested Asia Minor with him around 241-227 BC. With Galatian mercenaries he defeated Seleucus near Ancyra, and then, allied with them, lost several battles against Attalus I. He died in Thrace in 226 BC, at the hands of bandits according to Justin (XXVII.3); that they were Gauls is a modern reading.

personas/atalo-i/resumen.texto: Ruler of Pergamon from 241 to 197 BC, who refused to pay the Galatians the tribute they levied on the cities, defeated them by the springs of the Caicus and, according to Polybius (XVIII.41), took the title of king because of that victory. He celebrated his victories with the bronze monuments in the sanctuary of Athena at Pergamon and with an offering on the Acropolis of Athens (Pausanias I.25.2), from which the Roman copies of the Dying Gaul and the Ludovisi Gaul would come. He was an ally of Rome against Philip V of Macedonia, and in 204 BC he helped the Romans take the stone of the Great Mother from Pessinus (Livy XXIX.11).

personas/epigono-de-pergamo/resumen.texto: A sculptor at the court of Attalus I. Pliny the Elder (XXXIV.84 and 88) says that several artists depicted the battles of Attalus and Eumenes against the Galatians (in XXXIV.84 the manuscripts read “Isigonus”, which is usually emended to Epigonus), and he praises by Epigonus a trumpeter and a boy caressing his dead mother. His signature appears on bases on the terrace of Athena at Pergamon. For that reason the bronze originals of the Dying Gaul and the Ludovisi Gaul are attributed to him, a plausible but unproven attribution.

personas/eumenes-ii/resumen.texto: King of Pergamon from 197 to 159 BC, son of Attalus I. An ally of Rome against Antiochus III at Magnesia (190 BC), he received in the peace of Apamea almost all of Seleucid Asia Minor, and in 168-166 BC he defeated the Galatians, who had invaded his kingdom. In his reign the great altar of Pergamon was raised, whose frieze of the battle of the gods against the giants is often read as an allusion to those wars.

personas/ortiagon/resumen.texto: Chief of the Tolistoboii who, in 189 BC, led the resistance against Gnaeus Manlius Vulso on Mount Olympus together with Combolomarus and Gaulotus (Livy XXXVIII.19). Polybius (XXII.21) describes him as generous, prudent and brave, and says that he intended to unite all the Galatians under his command. His wife was Chiomara.

personas/quiomara/resumen.texto: Wife of Ortiagon. Captured in 189 BC by the troops of Manlius Vulso and raped by a centurion, she had her people kill him while he was collecting the ransom, and took his head to her husband. Polybius (XXI.38) says that he met her at Sardis and praises her intelligence; the story is repeated by Livy (XXXVIII.24) and Plutarch (Virtues of Women 22), who use it as a model of female virtue.

personas/epossognato/resumen.texto: A Galatian chief, the only one who remained a friend of Eumenes II in 189 BC. According to Polybius (XXI.37) and Livy (XXXVIII.18), he tried unsuccessfully to get the other Galatian kings to submit to Manlius Vulso.

personas/cneo-manlio-vulson/resumen.texto: Roman consul of 189 BC who conducted a campaign against the Galatians of Asia Minor for having helped Antiochus III, and defeated them on Mount Olympus and Magaba. The campaign is recounted by Livy (XXXVIII.12-27 and 44-50) and Polybius (XXI.33-39). Livy records the accusations of his enemies in the Senate, who denied him a triumph for having waged a war without authorization in order to plunder, and blames him for bringing the luxury of Asia to Rome (XXXIX.6). He celebrated his triumph in 187 BC.

personas/camma/resumen.texto: A Galatian, priestess of Artemis, wife of the tetrarch Sinatus. According to Plutarch (Virtues of Women 20 and Amatorius 22) and Polyaenus (VIII.39), Sinorix killed her husband in order to marry her; she agreed, drank with him in the temple from a poisoned cup, and both died. It cannot be dated with certainty (probably the 2nd or 1st century BC); it is a Greek moral story with Galatian names.

personas/deyotaro/resumen.texto: Tetrarch of the Tolistobogii and king of Galatia. An ally of Rome against Mithridates VI, he received from Pompey territories and the title of king; he fought with Pompey at Pharsalus, and Julius Caesar pardoned him but took away some of his lands. In 45 BC his grandson Castor accused him of having wanted to kill Caesar, and Cicero defended him in the speech Pro rege Deiotaro. Strabo (XII.5.3) tells that he concentrated the power of the tetrarchs in his own hands and that he killed his son-in-law and his daughter; Cicero (De divinatione I and II) tells that he undertook nothing without observing the flight of birds. Almost everything we know about him comes from Cicero, who was his friend and his advocate.

personas/castor-de-galacia/resumen.texto: Grandson of King Deiotarus through his daughter, who in 45 BC accused him before Julius Caesar of having planned to kill Caesar when he received him in Galatia in 47 BC. We know him through Cicero's speech Pro rege Deiotaro, which presents him as a disloyal grandson; his father was the tetrarch Castor Tarcondarius (Saocondarius in Strabo XII.5.3), son-in-law of Deiotarus, whom the king had killed together with his daughter.

personas/brogitaro/resumen.texto: Tetrarch of the Trocmi and son-in-law of Deiotarus, who in 58 BC obtained from Rome, by a law of the tribune Clodius, the title of king and the priesthood of the Great Mother of Pessinus. Cicero (On the Response of the Haruspices 28-29; Pro Sestio 56) presents him as a barbarian who bought titles and desecrated the sanctuary. He died around 50 BC.

personas/adiatorix/resumen.texto: Son of the Galatian tetrarch Domnecleo, who governed part of Heraclea Pontica by grant of Mark Antony and, shortly before the battle of Actium, had the Roman settlers of the city killed at night. Octavian took him in his triumph and had him executed along with one of his sons; this is told by Strabo (XII.3.6 and 3.35), who adds that another son, Diteutus, later became priest of Comana.

personas/amintas-de-galacia/resumen.texto: Last king of Galatia, formerly secretary to Deiotarus. Mark Antony made him king in 36 BC, and he went over to Octavian before Actium, so he kept the kingdom, enlarged toward Pisidia and Lycaonia. He died in 25 BC fighting the Homonadenses of the Taurus (Strabo XII.6.3; Cassius Dio LIII.26), and his kingdom became the Roman province of Galatia.

personas/ptolomeo-ii/resumen.texto: King of Egypt from 283 to 246 BC, son of Ptolemy I. He hired some four thousand Galatians and, when he learned they were plotting to seize Egypt, according to Pausanias (I.7.2) he left them on an island in the Nile, where they died of hunger or killed one another. The poet Callimachus celebrated that victory in the Hymn to Delos, comparing it with the defeat of the Gauls at Delphi.

personas/autarito/resumen.texto: Chief of the Gaulish mercenaries of Carthage, one of the leaders of the Mercenary War (241-237 BC) together with Spendius and Matho. Polybius (I.77-85) says that everyone listened to him because, after years of service, he spoke Phoenician, and that it was he who proposed torturing and killing the Carthaginian prisoners. Hamilcar Barca captured him and had him crucified in sight of Tunis.

personas/cincibil/resumen.texto: Gaulish king of the eastern Alps, probably of Noricum, who in 170 BC sent his brother to the Roman Senate to complain that the consul Gaius Cassius Longinus had sacked allied Alpine peoples and sold thousands of people into slavery. According to Livy (XLIII.5), the Senate agreed with him, disowned the consul, and sent gifts to the two brothers.

personas/critasiro/resumen.texto: King of the Boii of the middle Danube who, according to Strabo (VII.3.11 and 5.2), was defeated together with the Taurisci by the Dacian king Burebista around the middle of the 1st century BC. Strabo says the Boii were wiped out and their land was left as pasture; nothing else is known about him.

personas/burebista/resumen.texto: King of the Getae and Dacians who, around 82-44 BC, united a great kingdom north of the Danube. Strabo (VII.3.11 and 5.2) tells that he destroyed the Boii of Critasiro and the Taurisci, that he plundered Thrace as far as Macedonia and that, with the priest Decaeneus, he imposed discipline on his people to the point of making them uproot their vineyards. He was killed in a conspiracy around 44 BC, at the time of Caesar's assassination, and his kingdom was divided.

personas/voccio/resumen.texto: King of Noricum. Caesar (Gallic War I.53) tells that a sister of his was one of the two wives of Ariovistus and that she died in the flight after the defeat of 58 BC; in 49 BC a Noric king, who is usually identified with him, sent three hundred horsemen to Caesar (Civil War I.18). He is one of the few kings of Noricum known by name.

personas/maroboduo/resumen.texto: King of the Marcomanni who, around 9-6 BC, led his people to Bohemia, the former land of the Boii, and there built a powerful kingdom (Strabo VII.1.3; Velleius Paterculus II.108; Tacitus, Germania 42). Tiberius prepared a campaign against him in AD 6, which was suspended because of the revolt of Pannonia; overthrown in 19, he took refuge in Ravenna, where he lived until his death in 37 (Tacitus, Annals II.62-63).

personas/memnon-de-heraclea/resumen.texto: Greek historian of Heraclea Pontica, probably of the 1st or 2nd century AD, author of a history of his city that we know only through the summary of books IX to XVI made by the patriarch Photius in the 9th century. He is the closest source on the treaty between Nicomedes I and the Gauls who crossed into Asia.

personas/cirilo-de-escitopolis/resumen.texto: Monk and historian of the monks of Palestine in the 6th century. In the Life of Euthymius (55) he tells of a possessed Galatian monk who did not speak and who, when pressed, “spoke in Galatian”: it is the latest witness that Galatian was still spoken, although in isolation and disputed.

personas/pirro-de-epiro/resumen.texto: King of Epirus, known for his wars against Rome in Italy. In 274 BC he invaded Macedonia with Galatian mercenaries, who plundered the royal tombs of Aegae (Plutarch, Pyrrhus 26), and he dedicated to Athena Itonia the shields of the Galatians of Antigonus whom he had defeated, with an epigram preserved by Pausanias (I.13.2-3). He died at Argos in 272 BC.

personas/ninfis-de-heraclea/resumen.texto: Historian and politician of Heraclea Pontica of the 3rd century BC, who led the return of the exiles to his city in 281 BC and wrote a history of Heraclea. His work was lost, but Memnon used it, so what we know of the first Galatians in Asia ultimately comes from a contemporary.

personas/carl-humann/resumen.texto: German engineer who, while building roads in the Ottoman Empire, discovered and from 1878 excavated the acropolis of Pergamon and brought the reliefs of the great altar to Berlin, where it was reconstructed in the Pergamon Museum.

personas/manolis-andronikos/resumen.texto: Greek archaeologist who in 1977 found at Vergina, the ancient Aegae, intact Macedonian royal tombs beneath the great tumulus; he attributed one of them to Philip II, an identification that is disputed. He interpreted the tumulus as the work of Antigonus Gonatas, who covered the tombs after the plundering by the Galatians of Pyrrhus.

personas/william-mitchell-ramsay/resumen.texto: Scottish archaeologist who traveled through Asia Minor from 1880 and studied its historical geography and inscriptions. He argued that the Letter to the Galatians was addressed to the cities of the southern part of the Roman province and not to the ethnic Galatians of the north, the so-called South Galatian hypothesis, which is still debated.

personas/stephen-mitchell/resumen.texto: British historian and epigraphist of ancient Anatolia (1948-2024), professor at Swansea and Exeter, author of Anatolia: Land, Men, and Gods in Asia Minor (1993) and of the standard studies on the Galatians, based on epigraphy and fieldwork in Turkey.

personas/combutis/resumen.texto: Gaulish chief whom Brennus, together with Orestorio, sent in 279 BC to plunder Aetolia to force the Aetolians to leave Thermopylae. Pausanias (X.22.2-4), the only source, attributes to him the massacre at Calion.

personas/orestorio/resumen.texto: Gaulish chief who, together with Combutis, led the attack on Aetolia in 279 BC, according to Pausanias (X.22.2). Nothing else is known about him.

personas/combolomaro/resumen.texto: One of the three chiefs of the Tolistobogii, with Ortiagon and Gauloto, who in 189 BC took refuge on Mount Olympus before Manlius Vulso, according to Livy (XXXVIII.19).

personas/gauloto/resumen.texto: One of the three chiefs of the Tolistobogii, together with Ortiagon and Combolomaro, who in 189 BC resisted Manlius Vulso on Mount Olympus, according to Livy (XXXVIII.19).

personas/sinato/resumen.texto: Galatian tetrarch, husband of Camma, whom Sinorix killed in order to marry her, according to Plutarch (Bravery of Women 20 and Amatorius 22) and Polyaenus (VIII.39). He is known only from that story.

personas/sinorix/resumen.texto: Galatian tetrarch who, according to Plutarch and Polyaenus, killed Sinato in order to marry his widow Camma and died poisoned by her at the wedding ceremony. He is known only from that story, which Greek authors told as an example of marital fidelity.

personas/domnecleo/resumen.texto: Galatian tetrarch, father of Adiatorix, according to Strabo (XII.3.6). It is all that is known about him.

personas/bogodiatar/resumen.texto: Tetrarch of the Trocmi to whom Pompey, when he reorganized Asia Minor after the war against Mithridates, gave the city of Mithridation in Pontus, according to Strabo (XII.3.13).

personas/meleagro-de-macedonia/resumen.texto: Son of Ptolemy I Soter and brother of Ptolemy Ceraunus, he reigned in Macedonia for about two months in 279 BC, after Ceraunus died in combat against the Celts, until the Macedonians deposed him 'as unworthy', according to Eusebius (Chronicle, Book I, which follows Porphyry). His brief reign shows the power vacuum left by the Gallic invasion; the exact chronology of those months is uncertain.

personas/antipatro-etesias/resumen.texto: Nephew of Cassander, son of his brother Philip, he was king of Macedonia for 45 days in 279 BC, after the expulsion of Meleager. According to Eusebius (Chronicle, Book I, which follows Porphyry), Sosthenes 'put him to flight' at the end of those 45 days, and the nickname Etesias comes from the etesian winds, which blow roughly for the length of his reign. After Sosthenes' death, the partisans of Antipater, Ptolemy and Arrhidaeus disputed Macedonia, and 'while Antipater was conspiring, Antigonus took power.' A papyrus from the archive of Zenon, written in Alexandria in 258-256 BC (P.Cair.Zen. I 59019), names an 'Antipater the Etesias' in a private letter, in the time of Ptolemy II and with no hint of a claim to the throne. His death is unknown.

hechos/expansion-celta-a-la-cuenca-de-lo.texto: The Celts expand into the middle Danube and the Carpathian Basin

Archaeology shows that in the 4th century BC graves of warriors with swords and ornaments in the La Tène style, such as the brooches of the Duchcov type, spread from Austria and Bohemia into Hungary, Slovakia, Transylvania and northern Serbia. Justin (XXIV.4) speaks of three hundred thousand Gauls looking for land, part of whom settled in Pannonia, and Livy (V.34) tells it as the legendary journey of Segovesus to the Hercynian forests. How much of this was migration of people and how much local adoption of a fashion and of weapons is an open debate.

hechos/gran-invasion-celta-de-los-balcan.texto: The great Celtic invasion of Macedonia and Greece

After the deaths of Lysimachus and Seleucus (281 BC), which left the Danube frontier undefended, three Gaulish columns attacked in 280-279 BC: Cerethrius against the Thracians, Bolgius against Macedonia, where he killed King Ptolemy Ceraunus, and Brennus and Acichorius against Paeonia and Greece. Pausanias (X.19-23) and Justin (XXIV-XXV) recount the campaign with enormous figures, 152,000 infantry and 20,400 cavalry according to Pausanias, which no one takes literally; Pausanias (X.19.11) adds that each horseman rode with two servants on horseback, the trimarkisia, from marka, “horse” in the Gaulish language, one of the few Celtic words recorded by a Greek author. After Delphi the groups scattered: some returned to the Danube, others founded the Gaulish kingdom of Tylis in Thrace, and others crossed into Asia. The surviving accounts are Greek and late, and present the invasion as a new war against the Persians, with the Gauls in the role of impious barbarians.

hechos/derrota-de-ptolomeo-cerauno/titul.texto: The Gauls of Bolgius defeat and kill Ptolemy Ceraunus

hechos/derrota-de-ptolomeo-cerauno/resum.texto: The king of Macedonia went out to face the Gauls of Bolgius with few troops, after rejecting the help of twenty thousand Dardanians and despising the Gaulish envoys who offered peace in exchange for money, according to Justin (XXIV.4-5). Wounded and captured, he was beheaded and his head was carried around on a spear (Justin XXIV.5); Memnon (8.8), by contrast, tells that the elephant he rode was wounded and threw him, and that the Gauls captured him alive and tore him to pieces. Macedonia was without a king for almost two years and was plundered.

hechos/batalla-de-las-termopilas-279/res.texto: A Greek coalition of Boeotians, Phocians, Locrians, Aetolians, Megarians and Athenians, the latter under Callippus and with ships attacking from the coast, checked Brennus at the pass, according to Pausanias (X.19-22). Brennus sent a force to plunder Aetolia so that the Aetolians would leave the pass, and in the end, like the Persians in 480 BC, he surrounded the Greeks by the mountain path; the defenders withdrew by sea. Pausanias, who wrote about four and a half centuries later, builds the account in parallel with the defense of the pass against the Persians.

hechos/saqueo-de-calion/titulo.texto: The Gauls sack Calion, in Aetolia

hechos/saqueo-de-calion/resumen.texto: To force the Aetolians to leave Thermopylae, Brennus sent Combutis and Orestorio to attack Aetolia. Pausanias (X.22.2-4) describes the capture of Calion with the massacre of all the men, the old and the children, rapes and cannibalism, and says that the Aetolians, women included, pursued them in the retreat until they almost exterminated them. It is the most extreme passage in the Greek image of the barbarian, and it comes from an Aetolian tradition that, after the war, presented the Aetolians as the saviors of Greece.

hechos/ataque-galo-a-delfos/resumen.texto: Brennus reached Delphi at the end of 279 BC. Pausanias (X.23) and Justin (XXIV.7-8) tell that Apollo defended his sanctuary with an earthquake, lightning, a snowstorm and rocks falling from Parnassus, with the appearance of the heroes Hyperochus, Laodocus, Pyrrhus and Phylacus, and with a nighttime panic in which the Gauls killed one another; Brennus, wounded, killed himself. This is a pious account: the decree of Cos of 278 BC already attributes the victory to the god, but also to the men who came to defend the sanctuary. Modern historians give a more earthly explanation: the defense by the Phocians and Aetolians, the winter in the mountains and the lack of supplies of an army far from its land. The Greek texts say that the sanctuary was not plundered, and a later tradition, which Strabo already doubted, said that the gold of Delphi ended up in Tolosa.

hechos/soterias-de-delfos/titulo.texto: Founding of the Soteria at Delphi

hechos/soterias-de-delfos/resumen.texto: To celebrate the salvation of the sanctuary, the Soteria were instituted at Delphi, festivals with musical and athletic contests in honor of Apollo and Zeus Soter. Around 246 BC the Aetolians, who dominated Delphi, reorganized them as a Panhellenic festival and asked the other cities to recognize it. The surviving decrees of recognition, such as those of Athens and Chios, are the main source on how the invasion was remembered, and they show the political use the Aetolians made of their victory.

hechos/batalla-de-lisimaquia/resumen.texto: Antigonus Gonatas set an ambush for a Gaulish band near Lysimachia, in the Thracian Chersonese: he left his camp empty and, when the Gauls were plundering it, attacked and defeated them, according to Justin (XXV.1-2). The victory gave him the prestige to be acknowledged as king of Macedonia.

hechos/reino-de-tile/titulo.texto: Gaulish kingdom of Tylis, in Thrace

hechos/reino-de-tile/resumen.texto: The Gauls of Comontorius, who did not follow on toward Greece or Asia, founded a kingdom in eastern Thrace with its capital at Tylis, near the Haemus mountains, and collected tribute from Byzantium, which came to pay them eighty talents a year (Polybius IV.45-46). The kingdom lasted until, under its last king, Cavarus, the Thracians rose up and destroyed it around 212 BC. The location of Tylis is disputed (Tulovo, in Bulgaria, has been proposed): in Thrace there are scattered Celtic finds, but none identifies the capital.

hechos/escordiscos-en-el-danubio/titulo.texto: The Scordisci settle along the Sava and the Danube

hechos/escordiscos-en-el-danubio/resumen.texto: According to Justin (XXXII.3) and Athenaeus (VI.25, who follows Posidonius), part of those who attacked Delphi returned north with Bathanatos and settled at the confluence of the Sava and the Danube under the name Scordisci. Their main center was Singidunum, present-day Belgrade, whose name is Celtic. Ancient authors sometimes call them Celts, Thracians or Illyrians, and it is debated whether they were a Celtic people or a mixed confederation to which their neighbors gave a common name.

hechos/paso-de-los-galatas-a-asia/resume.texto: Some twenty thousand Gauls under Leonorius and Lutarius, of whom no more than half were warriors according to Livy (XXXVIII.16), crossed the Bosphorus and the Hellespont in 278-277 BC, hired by Nicomedes I of Bithynia, who needed them against Antiochus I and against his brother. Memnon of Heraclea (11) summarizes the pact: they would always support Nicomedes and his sons and would also fight for the allied Greek cities, such as Byzantium, Heraclea and Chalcedon. Afterwards they plundered western Asia Minor, as the decree of Priene in honor of Sotas shows, and according to Livy they divided the plundering areas: the Trocmi took the Hellespont, the Tolistobogii Aeolis and Ionia, the Tectosages the interior. They ended up settling in eastern Phrygia, which came to be called Galatia.

hechos/batalla-de-los-elefantes/resumen.texto: Antiochus I defeated the Galatians in a battle in Asia Minor that we know in detail only from Lucian (Zeuxis 8-11): his sixteen elephants frightened the horses of the Galatians, who were not used to them. Appian (Syriaca 65) says that for having expelled the Galatians Antiochus received the title Soter. The date, between 275 and 268 BC, and the place are unknown, and the victory did not eliminate the Galatians, who went on collecting tribute from the Greek cities.

hechos/motin-de-los-galatas-de-ptolomeo-.texto: Revolt of Ptolemy II's Galatian mercenaries

Ptolemy II had hired about four thousand Galatians for his war with his half-brother Magas of Cyrene; according to Pausanias (I.7.2), when he learned they planned to seize Egypt, he took them to a deserted island in the Nile, where they died of hunger or killed one another. Callimachus celebrated it in the Hymn to Delos (171-188), where Apollo, still in his mother's womb, prophesies the defeat of the Gauls at Delphi and that of those who would rise against Ptolemy. It is one of the first uses of the victory over the Galatians as royal propaganda, earlier than at Pergamon.

hechos/saqueo-de-las-tumbas-de-egas/titu.texto: Pyrrhus's Gaulish mercenaries plunder the royal tombs of Aegae

hechos/saqueo-de-las-tumbas-de-egas/resu.texto: When Pyrrhus of Epirus invaded Macedonia, he left a garrison of Galatian mercenaries in Aegae, the former capital, and they plundered the kings' tombs in search of gold and scattered the bones, according to Plutarch (Pyrrhus 26) and Diodorus (XXII.12); Pyrrhus did not punish them, and the Macedonians reproached him for it. At Vergina, the ancient Aegae, Manolis Andronikos found intact royal tombs in 1977 beneath a great tumulus which, in his interpretation, Antigonus Gonatas raised afterwards to protect them from further plundering.

hechos/guerra-de-los-mercenarios/resumen.texto: The mercenaries whom Carthage did not pay after the First Punic War rebelled with the support of the Libyans; among their leaders was the Gaul Autarito, and Polybius (I.65-88) presents it as a war “without truce” in which both sides committed atrocities. Polybius (II.7) also tells that a band of Gauls who had served Carthage at Eryx deserted to the Romans and plundered the temple of Aphrodite. It is the main source on the life of Celtic mercenaries in the western Mediterranean, told from the point of view of those who hired them.

hechos/traicion-de-fenice/titulo.texto: The Gaulish mercenaries hand Phoenice over to the Illyrians

hechos/traicion-de-fenice/resumen.texto: Eight hundred Gauls, the same ones who had served Carthage and deserted at Eryx, were garrisoning Phoenice, the richest city in Epirus, and handed it over to the pirates of the Illyrian queen Teuta, according to Polybius (II.5-7). Polybius uses the episode as a lesson on why defense should not be entrusted to barbarian mercenaries, an idea common among Greek authors.

hechos/batalla-de-ancira/resumen.texto: In the war between the two Seleucid brothers, Antiochus Hierax, with Galatian mercenaries, defeated Seleucus II near Ancyra, and Seleucus barely escaped. According to Justin (XXVII.2), the Galatians, believing Seleucus dead, turned against Hierax, who had to buy his life with gold. It shows the weight of the Galatians as hired troops in the wars between kings.

hechos/victorias-de-atalo-sobre-los-gala.texto: Attalus I's victories over the Galatians

Attalus of Pergamon, the first to refuse to pay the tribute that the Galatians collected in Asia according to Livy (XXXVIII.16), defeated the Tolistobogii at the sources of the Caicus around 238 BC and then, in several battles, the Galatians allied with Antiochus Hierax. Polybius (XVIII.41) says that this victory over the most feared and warlike people of Asia was the basis of his royal title, and his own dedications at Pergamon celebrate it. The sources do not allow the battle to be dated precisely, which is placed between 241 and 233 BC

hechos/monumentos-de-pergamo/titulo.texto: The monuments of Pergamon against the Galatians

hechos/monumentos-de-pergamo/resumen.texto: The Attalids turned their victories over the Galatians into state art: bronze groups in the sanctuary of Athena at Pergamon, of which the Roman copies considered most likely are the Dying Galatian (Capitoline Museums) and the Ludovisi Galatian, who kills his wife and then himself (Palazzo Altemps), and an offering on the Athenian Acropolis with figures of giants, Amazons, Persians and defeated Galatians (Pausanias I.25.2). Pliny (XXXIV.84) names the sculptors. The type of the nude Galatian, with torque, mustache and matted hair, fixed the image of the Celt in ancient art and presented it as chaos defeated by the Greeks. Miranda Marvin (2002) argued that the statues in Rome are not copies of those bronzes and considered them Roman creations of the 2nd century AD; the most widespread opinion still sees them as derived, more or less freely, from originals from Pergamon.

hechos/altar-de-pergamo/titulo.texto: Construction of the great altar of Pergamon

hechos/altar-de-pergamo/resumen.texto: Eumenes II had a monumental altar built on the acropolis of Pergamon, with a frieze of more than one hundred meters showing the battle of the gods against the giants. Many historians read it as an allegory of Pergamon's victories over the Galatians, although no surviving inscription says so. Carl Humann excavated it from 1878, and it was reconstructed in Berlin, in the Pergamon Museum.

hechos/guerra-galata-de-manlio-vulson/re.texto: After defeating Antiochus III at Magnesia, where the Galatians had fought in his army, the consul Gnaeus Manlius Vulso marched against them in 189 BC and defeated them on Mount Olympus, where the Tolistobogii had taken refuge, and on Mount Magaba, near Ancyra, where the Tectosages and the Trocmi were. Livy (XXXVIII.12-27), who follows Polybius (XXI.33-39), tells that the Galatians fought almost naked and without throwing weapons, and fell under javelins and slings; for the dead on the Olympus he gives widely differing figures, from ten thousand to forty thousand, depending on the annalist he follows. In the Senate, Manlius's enemies accused him of having waged an unauthorized war for plunder (Livy XXXVIII.44-50), and the First Book of the Maccabees (8.2) counts his wars against the Galatians among the Roman feats.

hechos/guerra-de-eumenes-ii-contra-los-g.texto: War of Eumenes II against the Galatians

The Galatians invaded the kingdom of Pergamon in 168 BC, and Eumenes II defeated them in 166 BC. Polybius (XXX.28) tells that the Roman Senate, which already distrusted Eumenes, declared the Galatians autonomous on condition that they did not leave their territory. A fragment of Diodorus (XXXI.13) says that a Galatian chief, after a victory, sacrificed the youngest and most handsome of the prisoners to the gods: it is one of the ancient testimonies of human sacrifice among the Galatians, written by authors from the enemy side.

hechos/matanza-de-los-tetrarcas-galatas/.texto: Mithridates VI has the Galatian tetrarchs killed

Distrusting his Galatian allies, Mithridates VI of Pontus had the tetrarchs at his court killed, together with their wives and children; only three escaped, according to Appian (Mithridatica 46). The survivors, among them Deiotarus, sided with Rome, and the massacre sped up the concentration of Galatian power in a few hands.

hechos/galatas-de-cleopatra-para-herodes.texto: Augustus gives Herod Cleopatra's Galatian guard

After Cleopatra's death, Augustus gave Herod the four hundred Galatians who had been the queen's personal guard, according to Josephus (Jewish War I.397; Jewish Antiquities XV.217). Josephus names them again, along with Thracians and Germans, among the troops at Herod's funeral (Jewish War I.672). It shows that the Galatians went on serving as elite troops of the Hellenistic kings until the end of those kingdoms.

hechos/provincia-de-galacia/resumen.texto: On the death of King Amyntas in 25 BC, Augustus did not recognize his heirs and turned the kingdom into a province, with its capital at Ancyra (Cassius Dio LIII.26). The province added Pisidia, Lycaonia and other lands of the south to the Galatia of the three tribes, which explains the debate over whom Paul wrote to. The tribes continued to exist as communities centered on Ancyra (Tectosages), Pessinus (Tolistobogii) and Tavium (Trocmi), and their nobles became priests of the imperial cult.

hechos/mision-de-pablo-en-galacia/resume.texto: According to the Acts of the Apostles (16.6 and 18.23), Paul crossed “the Phrygian and Galatian region” on his second and third journeys, and his Letter to the Galatians, from around 50-57, is addressed to communities he had founded. Since the 19th century it has been debated whether they were the northern Galatians, around Ancyra, Pessinus and Tavium, as the Church Fathers understood, or the cities of the south of the province, such as Antioch of Pisidia, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe, as William Ramsay argued. The letter gives no sign that its recipients were Celts.

hechos/galata-en-tiempos-de-jeronimo/tit.texto: Jerome compares the Galatian language with that of the Treveri

hechos/galata-en-tiempos-de-jeronimo/res.texto: In the prologue to book II of his commentary on the Letter to the Galatians, written in Bethlehem around 387, Jerome says that the Galatians, besides the Greek spoken throughout the East, have a language of their own almost identical to that of the Treveri. Jerome had lived in Trier and passed through Ancyra, so he could have heard both languages; it is debated whether Gaulish was still spoken in Trier in the 4th century and whether Jerome was repeating an earlier source. It is, in any case, the last testimony of someone who knew both regions.

hechos/ultimo-testimonio-del-galata/titu.texto: The last witness to the spoken Galatian

hechos/ultimo-testimonio-del-galata/resu.texto: Cyril of Scythopolis, in the Life of Euthymius (55), written around 556, tells that a possessed Galatian monk did not speak and that, if pressed, he “spoke in Galatian” (Γαλατιστὶ ἐφθέγγετο). It is the last mention of someone who spoke Galatian, but it is an account of a miracle, without a single word of the language, and it cannot be ruled out that “Galatian” designated only a local speech. Since the language left almost nothing written, it is not known when it ceased to be spoken; in Galatia Greek ended up prevailing, and from the 11th century Turkish.

hechos/oro-de-los-tauriscos/resumen.texto: Polybius, quoted by Strabo (IV.6.12), tells that in his time gold was discovered among the Noric Taurisci, near Aquileia, so pure and so close to the surface that, when the Italians joined in the mining, the price of gold fell by a third throughout Italy within two months; then the Taurisci drove them out and worked the deposit alone. It is one of the few concrete economic facts about the Celts of the eastern Alps.

hechos/embajada-de-cincibil/titulo.texto: Embassy of King Cincibil to the Roman Senate

hechos/embajada-de-cincibil/resumen.texto: In 170 BC an embassy from Cincibil, a Gaulish king of the eastern Alps, arrived in Rome to complain that the consul Gaius Cassius Longinus had attacked Alpine peoples friendly to Rome and sold thousands of them into slavery. According to Livy (XLIII.5), the Senate disowned the consul and sent gifts to the king and his brother. It is one of the first reports of dealings between Rome and the kings of the eastern Alps, who are usually identified with the future kingdom of Noricum.

hechos/guerras-de-roma-contra-los-escord.texto: From Macedonia, a Roman province since 146 BC, Rome clashed for half a century with the Scordisci, who raided to the south. In 114 BC they defeated the consul Gaius Porcius Cato (Livy, Periochae 63); later they were defeated by Marcus Minucius Rufus, around 107 BC, and by Lucius Cornelius Scipio Asiaticus, who around 84 BC pushed them back across the Danube according to Appian (Illyrica 5). Florus (I.39), who counts them among the Thracians, and Ammianus (XXVII.4.4) describe them as the cruelest of barbarians, who sacrificed prisoners and drank from skulls: it is the usual portrait of the frontier enemy, written centuries later.

hechos/derrota-de-los-boyos-ante-burebis.texto: Burebista destroys the Boii and the Taurisci

Around the middle of the 1st century BC the Dacian king Burebista defeated the Boii of Critasiro and the Taurisci and, according to Strabo (VII.3.11 and 5.2), destroyed them and left their land as pasture for sheep. Pliny (III.146) calls that area, near Lake Pelso (Balaton), “the deserts of the Boii”. The coins with the legend BIATEC from the oppidum of Bratislava, which many date after that war, suggest that the Boii did not disappear altogether; the chronology is debated.

hechos/marcomanos-ocupan-bohemia/titulo.texto: The Marcomanni of Maroboduus settle in Bohemia

hechos/marcomanos-ocupan-bohemia/resumen.texto: Around 9-6 BC Maroboduus led the Marcomanni from the Main region to Bohemia, from which the Boii had already left, and founded a kingdom there (Strabo VII.1.3; Velleius Paterculus II.108; Tacitus, Germania 42). Tacitus (Germania 28) says that the name Boihaemum still recalled the Boii although the inhabitants had changed, and that is where “Bohemia” comes from. The relation between the arrival of the Germanic peoples and the abandonment of the Celtic oppida of Bohemia, such as Stradonice and Závist, is debated.

hechos/conquista-romana-del-norico-y-ret.texto: Roman conquest of the Alps, Raetia and Noricum

Cassius Dio (LIV.20) tells that in 16 BC Pannonians and Norici invaded Istria and were driven back, and that Noricum then came under Roman control: the kingdom, which had traded with Rome for a century, was annexed without a conquest recounted by the sources and became a province under Claudius. In the summer of 15 BC Drusus and Tiberius, stepsons of Augustus, subdued the Raeti and the Vindelici with two armies that advanced from Italy and from Gaul, with a battle on Lake Constance (Cassius Dio LIV.22; Strabo IV.6.9; Horace, Odes IV.4 and IV.14). The trophy of La Turbie (7-6 BC) celebrated the whole as a single victory of Augustus, and the Res Gestae (26) state that the Alps were pacified without waging an unjust war on any people.

hechos/saqueo-del-oppidum-de-stradonice/.texto: The discovery of Stradonice gold and the sack of the oppidum

In 1877 a deposit of Celtic gold coins was found at the oppidum of Stradonice, in central Bohemia, and the news set off a wave of clandestine digging that for years disturbed the site and scattered thousands of objects among collectors and museums. What was recovered, published by Josef Ladislav Píč in 1903 (in French, in 1906), remains one of the foundations for knowledge of the Bohemian oppida, but without archaeological context.

hechos/hallazgo-del-tesoro-de-duchcov/re.texto: In 1882, while working at a spring in Duchcov, in northern Bohemia, workers found a bronze cauldron with more than two thousand ornaments: brooches, bracelets and rings of bronze from the 4th century BC. It is interpreted as an offering in water, a practice well documented among the Celts; the pieces were scattered among museums and collectors before they were studied.

hechos/hallazgo-de-la-tumba-de-ciumesti/.texto: Discovery of the warrior's grave at Ciumești

In 1961 the grave of a Celtic warrior appeared at Ciumești, in northwestern Romania, with an iron helmet crowned by a bronze bird of prey with movable wings, a mail shirt and greaves. It is dated to the 3rd century BC and is part of a Celtic cemetery excavated in the 1960s, one of the testimonies of the Celtic presence in Transylvania and the Tisza basin. The helmet recalls the bird-crested helmets on the Gundestrup cauldron.

hechos/excavaciones-de-manching/titulo.texto: Excavations at the oppidum of Manching

hechos/excavaciones-de-manching/resumen.texto: Systematic excavations began in 1955 with Werner Krämer, on account of the expansion of a military airfield, and continued with Ferdinand Maier and Susanne Sievers; even so, they cover a small part of the site's 380 hectares. They brought to light streets, houses, workshops for iron, bronze, glass and coinage, and a murus gallicus rampart 7.2 kilometers long. In 1999 a hoard of 483 gold coins and an ingot appeared, the largest find of Celtic gold of the 20th century in Germany.

hechos/robo-del-oro-de-manching/titulo.texto: Theft of the Manching gold hoard

hechos/robo-del-oro-de-manching/resumen.texto: In the early hours of 22 November 2022 a gang cut fiber-optic cables in the area to block the alarm, forced a door of the Celtic and Roman Museum of Manching and took the 1999 treasure: 483 Celtic gold coins and a melted gold ingot, almost four kilograms. In July 2023 the police arrested four men from Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and found eighteen pieces of melted gold, equivalent to seventy-two coins. On 29 July 2025 the Ingolstadt Regional Court sentenced the four, for this and for other forced entries, to terms of between four years and nine months and eleven years, although it acquitted one of them of the Manching theft; the Federal Court of Justice confirmed the convictions in August 2026. The rest of the coins have still not turned up.

hechos/batalla-de-rafia/titulo.texto: Galatians at the battle of Raphia

hechos/batalla-de-rafia/resumen.texto: At the battle of Raphia, in which Ptolemy IV defeated Antiochus III, the Egyptian army included, according to Polybius (V.65.10), four thousand Thracians and Galatians descended from the soldiers settled in Egypt, and two thousand more recently recruited. It shows that the Galatians had become a stable military population of Ptolemaic Egypt, like the mercenaries who a few decades later left their graffiti at Abydos.

hechos/batalla-de-magnesia/titulo.texto: Galatians at the battle of Magnesia

hechos/batalla-de-magnesia/resumen.texto: Antiochus III faced the Romans of Lucius Cornelius Scipio with an army that, according to Livy (XXXVII.40), included Galatian cavalry and infantry, whom the Romans called Gallo-Greeks. The Seleucid defeat gave Rome the pretext for Manlius Vulso's campaign against the Galatians the following year.

hechos/reorganizacion-de-pompeyo-en-gala.texto: At the end of the war against Mithridates, Pompey reorganized Asia Minor: he confirmed the Galatian tetrarchs who had been loyal to Rome and gave Deiotarus lands in Pontus and in Lesser Armenia (Strabo XII.3.13; Appian, Mithridatica 114). It was the beginning of Deiotarus's rise, which the Senate later recognized as king.

hechos/legion-de-deyotaro/resumen.texto: Deiotarus armed and trained, in the Roman manner, an infantry force that the Alexandrian War (34) describes as a legion; Pharnaces of Pontus defeated it at Nicopolis in 48 BC, and troops of Deiotarus took part in Caesar's victory at Zela in 47 BC. When Galatia became a province, those troops became the XXII Deiotariana legion, which served in Egypt until it disappeared in the 2nd century, perhaps in the Bar Kokhba revolt. It is an early example of a Celtic army turned into a Roman unit.

hechos/defensa-de-deyotaro/resumen.texto: In November 45 BC Julius Caesar heard, at his house, Castor's accusation against his grandfather, King Deiotarus, for having wanted to kill him in 47 BC, and Cicero's defense. Caesar did not pass sentence before he died in March 44 BC; according to Cicero (Philippics II.93-95), Mark Antony afterwards sold to Deiotarus's envoys the restoration of his lands.

hechos/reino-del-norico/resumen.texto: Between the 2nd century BC and the Roman annexation, the peoples of the eastern Alps, with the Norici at their head, formed a kingdom that the Romans called regnum Noricum, centered on Magdalensberg. Livy (XLIII.5) records the embassy of Cincibil in 170 BC, who is usually held to have been a Noric king, and Caesar names their king Voccio and received Noric horsemen in 49 BC. It lived off the trade in its iron and gold with Italy through Aquileia, and passed to Rome without a conquest recounted by the sources.

hechos/boyos-sitian-noreia/titulo.texto: The Boii besiege Noreia and join the Helvetii

hechos/boyos-sitian-noreia/resumen.texto: Caesar (Gallic War I.5) tells that a group of Boii who had lived across the Rhine had moved into Noricum and besieged Noreia, and that the Helvetii added them to their migration of 58 BC; the siege was therefore earlier than that date, which is not known exactly. After the defeat at Bibracte, the Aedui settled them in their territory, where they reappear in 52 BC in their town of Gorgobina (I.28; VII.9).

hechos/helvecios-entre-el-rin-y-el-meno/.texto: The Helvetii between the Rhine, the Main and the Hercynian Forest

Tacitus (Germania 28) says that the Helvetii had earlier lived between the Hercynian Forest, the Rhine and the Main, with the Boii beyond them, and that both were Gallic peoples; Claudius Ptolemy (Geography II.11) marks a “desert of the Helvetii” north of the upper Danube. It is usually understood that the Helvetii left southern Germany for the Switzerland in which Caesar found them, but neither Tacitus nor Ptolemy gives a date, and archaeology does not allow us to fix when or why.

hechos/cotinos-hablan-galo/titulo.texto: The Cotini, Celts who speak Gaulish among the Germans

hechos/cotinos-hablan-galo/resumen.texto: Tacitus (Germania 43) says that the Gaulish language of the Cotini proves they are not Germans, that they pay tribute to the Sarmatians and the Quadi and that, “to their greater shame”, they extract iron. It is one of the few testimonies of a Celtic community that kept its language in central Europe at the end of the 1st century AD; archaeology links it to the Púchov culture, in northern Slovakia, a probable but not certain identification.

hechos/perseo-pierde-a-los-mercenarios-g.texto: By the Axius (Vardar), between Almana and Bylazora (Paeonia)

In the Third Macedonian War, a Gallic force of infantry and cavalry under a leader whom Livy (XLIV.26-27) calls Clondicus, waiting at Desudaba (Médica), offered its services to Perseus in exchange for money. Perseus left his camp at Elpeus and camped at Almana, by the Axius, to meet them. Livy calls them Gauls 'spread through Illyricum', who turned back 'to the Ister' (the Danube); Plutarch (Aemilius Paullus 12.2) calls them Bastarnae, a people whose language (Celtic or Germanic) is disputed. According to Livy, the king, out of greed, wanted to hire only 5,000 horsemen and did not bring the agreed gold, and the Gauls left, laying waste part of Thrace; Livy holds that this force would have put the Romans in serious difficulty. This is the account of the victors: Livy and Plutarch probably both follow Polybius.

hechos/el-sacerdote-de-pesinunte-habla-e.texto: The priest of Pessinus comes to Rome

In 102 BC a Bataces, priest of the Great Mother at Pessinus, a city in the territory of the Galatian Tolistoboii, traveled to Rome. According to Plutarch (Marius 17.5-6), he announced that the goddess promised victory to Rome; the Senate voted a temple for her, but the tribune Aulus Pompeius threw him off the Rostra, calling him an impostor, and died of fever within a week, which lent credibility to the priest. According to Diodorus (XXXVI.13, preserved in Photius's summary), Bataces demanded redress for the desecration of his temple and addressed the Senate wearing a golden crown and an embroidered cloak. The goddess's stone had come to Rome from Pessinus in 205-204 BC (Livy XXIX.10-14); the cult of Cybele was Phrygian, not Celtic, and the Tolistoboii had settled in the area around 270 BC.

hechos/el-galata-en-el-siglo-ii/resumen.texto: Around 170, two Greek authors report that Celtic was spoken in Asia Minor. Pausanias (X.36.1) says that the shrub the Greeks call kokkos, the kermes oak, is called hys 'in their language' by the Galatians beyond Phrygia; Lucian (Alexander 51) tells how Alexander of Abonoteichos answered oracles to anyone who asked 'in Syriac or in Celtic'. Neither gives more words or says how many people spoke it, and Lucian does not say those Celts were Galatians; two centuries later Jerome compares it with the language of the Treveri.

lugares/ancira/resumen.texto: Phrygian city that from the 3rd century BC was the center of the Tectosages Galatians and from 25 BC the capital of the Roman province of Galatia. Its temple of Augustus and Roma preserves the most complete copy of the Res Gestae of Augustus. It is present-day Ankara, the capital of Turkey.

lugares/templo-de-augusto-y-roma-de-anci.texto: Temple of Augustus and Roma at Ancyra

Temple of the imperial cult at Ancyra, on whose walls the text of the Res Gestae of Augustus was engraved after AD 14, in Latin and in Greek. An inscription on its walls lists the priests of the imperial cult, Galatian nobles such as Pylaemenes, son of King Amyntas, and shows how the old aristocracy of the tribes became the elite of the Roman province.

lugares/pesinunte/resumen.texto: Phrygian city with the sanctuary of the Great Mother (Cybele), from which in 204 BC the Romans took the goddess's black stone (Livy XXIX.10-11). It was the center of the Tolistobogii Galatians, and its priesthood was so powerful that Brogitarus bought it in Rome in 58 BC. Belgian excavations from 1967 brought to light the temple and the Roman city.

lugares/gordion/resumen.texto: Former capital of the Phrygian kingdom, on the Sangarius River, the city of Alexander's Gordian knot. In the Galatian period it was a minor village; excavations by the University of Pennsylvania found in its 3rd- and 2nd-century BC levels human and animal remains in deposits that the excavator Mary Voigt interpreted as possible sacrifices in the Celtic manner. That reading rests on analogy with the classical texts and is debated.

lugares/tavio/resumen.texto: Center of the Trocmi Galatians, east of the Halys River, next to the present-day Turkish village of Büyüknefes. Strabo (XII.5.2) says that it was the market of the region and that it had a bronze colossus of Zeus and a sacred precinct with right of asylum.

lugares/pergamo/resumen.texto: City of Mysia, in western Asia Minor, capital of the kingdom of the Attalids from 282 to 133 BC, when the last king bequeathed it to Rome. Its kings presented themselves as defenders of the Greeks against the Galatians and showed it in their art, with the monuments of the sanctuary of Athena and the great altar.

lugares/manching/resumen.texto: Large Celtic oppidum on the Danube, near Ingolstadt (Bavaria), which began as a village in the 3rd century BC and was walled in the 2nd, until it covered 380 hectares with a 7.2-kilometer rampart. It is estimated that between five and ten thousand people lived there; perhaps it was the center of the Vindelici, but its ancient name is unknown. It was abandoned around 50-30 BC, before the Roman conquest.

lugares/zavist/resumen.texto: The largest oppidum in the Czech Republic, on a hill above the Vltava, south of Prague, with about 170 hectares. Before becoming an oppidum, in the 6th to 4th centuries BC, it had an acropolis with a sacred enclosure and buildings interpreted as temples, contemporary with the princely centers of Hallstatt. The Archaeological Institute of Prague excavated it from 1963 to 1989; Karla Motyková, Petr Drda and Alena Rybová published its walls, its gates and the acropolis (Drda and Rybová, 2008).

lugares/stradonice/resumen.texto: Oppidum of about 90 hectares on the Berounka River, in central Bohemia, one of the richest production and trade centers of the Boii in the 1st century BC, with workshops for coins, glass and metal and imports from Italy. It was plundered from 1877 by treasure hunters and by Josef Ladislav Píč, who published what was recovered and identified it with Marobudum, the capital of Maroboduus, an idea now abandoned.

lugares/oppidum-de-bratislava/resumen.texto: Oppidum of the Boii on the castle hill of Bratislava and its surroundings, from the late 2nd and the 1st century BC. Silver coins with legends in Latin letters were struck there, such as BIATEC and NONNOS, among the earliest Celtic names written in central Europe; it is debated whether they were kings or magistrates. On the castle hill, stone buildings in the Roman technique were found, built for the Celtic elite.

lugares/gellert/resumen.texto: Hill in Budapest, next to the Danube, where in the 1st century BC there was the oppidum of the Eravisci. The Eravisci struck silver coins with their name (RAVIS, IRAVSCI) and, after the Roman conquest, came down to the plain, next to the camp and the Roman city of Aquincum.

lugares/magdalensberg/resumen.texto: Mountain in Carinthia (Austria) where from the late 2nd century BC there was a center of the kingdom of Noricum and a quarter of Roman merchants who bought iron, the “Noric iron” famous in Rome (Ovid, Metamorphoses XIV.712; Horace, Odes I.16.9). Graffiti on the walls of its houses record purchases of iron and other goods. It was abandoned in the mid-1st century AD, when Claudius founded Virunum on the plain.

lugares/durrnberg/resumen.texto: Mountain next to Hallein (Austria) with salt mines worked from the 6th century BC and a large Celtic settlement and cemetery, with rich early La Tène graves such as the one with the bronze jug with a spout. It is, together with Hallstatt, the great salt-producing center of the eastern Alps.

lugares/singiduno/resumen.texto: Fortress of the Scordisci at the confluence of the Sava and the Danube, whose name contains the Celtic element -dunum, “fortress”. From the end of the 1st century it was the base of the IV Flavia legion and a Roman city, and it is present-day Belgrade, the capital of Serbia.
